intro: Buddhists all over the world tell a story about a prince named Siddhartha. He lived in India long ago. He had a palace and everything he wanted. But he had a big question.

In this unit you will hear his story as Buddhists tell it. You will learn about the Four Sights, a bowl of rice, and a tree. You will be able to retell the story in order and say what the middle way means.
bigQuestion: Why did a prince leave his palace, and what did Buddhists say he found?

timeline.t: Prince Siddhartha lives in a palace with high walls.
He rides out and sees a sick man and an old man.
He sees a funeral and a calm holy man.
He leaves the palace to find an answer.
He tries being very hungry, and it does not help.
Sujata gives him a bowl of rice.
Buddhists believe he awakens under the Bodhi tree and becomes the Buddha.

words.d: the son of a king and queen
a very big house where a king or queen lives
the sick man, old man, funeral and holy man the prince saw
to hurt or feel sad
knowing what is true and good
the path between too much and too little
a title meaning "the awakened one"
the tree where Buddhists believe the Buddha awakened

test.q: What was Siddhartha before he became the Buddha?
test.why: Buddhists tell that he was a prince in a palace.

test.q: Why did the king build high walls?
test.why: The story says the king wanted his son to see only happy things.

test.q: Which is one of the Four Sights?
test.why: The Four Sights are a sick man, an old man, a funeral and a holy man.

test.q: What question did the prince ask?
test.why: The sights made him wonder why people suffer.
Channa drove the prince's cart in the story.

test.q: Who gave the tired man rice?
test.why: Buddhists tell that Sujata gave him rice cooked in milk.

choices: not too much, not too little
test.why: Buddhists say the middle way is between too much and too little.

test.q: Where did Buddhists say he awakened?
choices: in a cave by the sea
test.why: Buddhists believe he awakened under the Bodhi tree.
Buddha is a title that means the awakened one.

test.q: How do visitors show respect at Bodh Gaya?
test.why: Buddhists show respect at the Bodhi tree with bows and flowers.

write.prompt: Why did the prince leave the palace? Tell it in two or three sentences. Name one of the Four Sights and what Buddhists say he found under the Bodhi tree.
tips: Use the words middle way or Buddha.
Tell it in order: first, next, last.

title: The Prince Who Asked Why

chapters.title: Siddhartha Sees the World
chapters.bigQuestion: What did the prince see outside the palace, and why did it make him ask why?

story.title: Outside the Palace Gate
story.kicker: A prince rides out and sees something new.
paragraphs: Buddhists tell this story. Long ago, a prince named Siddhartha lived in a big palace. He had gardens, music and good food. His father wanted him to be happy every day.
One day the prince rode out of the palace gate. His driver was named Channa. On the road, the prince saw a man with white hair and a bent back. He walked slowly with a stick.
"Who is that?" the prince asked. "That is an old man," said Channa. "Everyone grows old one day." The prince was quiet. He had never seen an old person before.
That night the prince did not sleep well. He kept thinking. Why do people grow old? Why do people get hurt? He wanted to know.
story.think: What question would you ask if you saw something for the very first time?

lessons.title: A Prince Named Siddhartha
lessons.mainIdea: Buddhists tell of a prince named Siddhartha who lived long ago in India.
reading: Buddhists tell a story about a boy named Siddhartha. He lived about 2,500 years ago. His home was in the north of India, near Nepal today.
His father was a king. His mother was a queen named Maya. Siddhartha was a prince. He would grow up to be called the Buddha.

words.d: the son of a king and queen

look.title: Picture the Palace
look.text: Look at a big palace with tall walls. Inside are green gardens and a pond with flowers. A boy sits by the pond. He has everything he could want.
look.prompt: What would you like to see if you lived in this palace?

check.why: The Buddhist story says Siddhartha was a prince, the son of a king.
The story takes place in northern India about 2,500 years ago.
Buddhists tell that Queen Maya was his mother. Channa was his driver.

lessons.title: Walls All Around
lessons.mainIdea: The story says the king kept sad things away from his son.
reading: The king loved his son. The story says he wanted the prince to see only happy things. So the palace had high walls.
Inside the walls, no one was sick or old where the prince could see. Siddhartha did not know about sadness yet. Buddhists say he had never seen it.

words.d: a very big house where a king or queen lives

look.title: Only Happy Things
look.text: Look at the prince in his garden. Music plays. Flowers bloom. Every face he sees is smiling. Outside the wall, the town is busy with all kinds of people.
look.prompt: What might the prince not know about, if he only sees his garden?

check.q: Why did the palace have high walls?
check.why: The story says the king wanted his son to see only happy things.
Buddhists tell that he had never seen sadness inside the palace.

check.q: Who built the walls to keep sad things out?
check.why: The story says his father, the king, wanted to protect him.

lessons.title: A Sick Man and an Old Man
lessons.mainIdea: Outside the walls, the prince saw a sick man and an old man.
reading: Buddhists tell that the prince went outside the walls. First he saw a man who was very sick. Then he saw a man who was very old.
The prince was surprised. His driver said that all people can get sick. All people grow old. The prince felt sad for them.

words.d: not feeling well in your body

look.title: On the Road
look.text: Look at the dusty road. An old man walks with a stick. Nearby, a sick man rests by a tree. The prince stops his cart to look.
look.prompt: How do you think the prince felt? What face would he make?

check.q: What did the prince see first outside?
check.why: In the story he saw a sick man and an old man.

check.q: What did the driver tell him?
choices: all people can get sick and old
check.why: Channa said sickness and old age come to everyone.
The story says he felt sad and began to wonder.

lessons.title: A Funeral and a Calm Man
lessons.mainIdea: Next he saw a funeral, and then a calm holy man.
reading: Next the prince saw people carrying a man who had died. His family was crying. This was a funeral. The prince felt very sad.
Last, he saw a holy man in a plain robe. The man looked calm and peaceful. Buddhists call these four the Four Sights.

words.d: quiet and peaceful inside
the sick man, old man, funeral and holy man the prince saw

look.title: The Four Sights
look.cite: Buddhist life stories of the Buddha, such as the Jataka's opening story (Nidanakatha)

check.q: What did the prince see last?
check.why: In the Four Sights, the calm holy man comes last.
Buddhists call them the Four Sights.

check.q: How did the holy man look?
check.why: The story says the holy man was calm, and this gave the prince an idea.

lessons.title: A Big Question
lessons.mainIdea: The prince wondered why people suffer.
reading: The prince kept thinking about what he saw. Why do people get sick? Why do they grow old? Why are people sad?
Buddhists say he wanted to find a way to help. He wanted to understand suffering. Suffering means hurting or feeling sad.

words.d: to hurt or feel sad

look.title: Wondering
look.text: Look at the prince sitting by his window at night. The moon is bright. He is not playing. He is thinking hard about the people he saw.
look.prompt: What is one big question you wonder about?

check.q: What did the prince want to know?
check.why: The story says the Four Sights made him ask why people suffer.
Suffer means to hurt or feel sad.
Buddhists say he wanted to find a way to help.

lessons.title: Leaving the Palace
lessons.mainIdea: Buddhists tell that the prince left the palace to find an answer.
reading: One night the prince made a hard choice. He left the palace. He left his fine clothes and his riches.
Buddhists tell that he wanted to find an answer to his question. He became a traveler looking for wisdom. His search had begun.

words.d: knowing what is true and good

look.title: Two Kinds of Asking
look.text: Some questions have quick answers, like "What is for lunch?" Some questions take a long time, like "Why are people sad?" The prince asked a long-time question.
look.prompt: Can you think of a quick question and a long-time question?

check.q: What did the prince leave behind?
check.why: The story says he left the palace and his riches to search.
Buddhists tell that he left to answer his question about suffering.

choices: knowing what is true and good
check.why: Wisdom means knowing what is true and good.

review.why: The story says Siddhartha was a prince, so his father was a king.
The Four Sights are the sick man, old man, funeral and holy man.

review.q: Which sight made the prince feel hopeful?
review.why: The calm holy man showed him a peaceful way to live.
The Four Sights led him to ask why people suffer.
This is the story Buddhists tell about the Buddha's life.

review.q: What did the prince do at the end?
review.why: He left the palace to search for an answer.

chapters.title: Under the Bodhi Tree
chapters.bigQuestion: How did Siddhartha find a middle way, and what happened under the tree?

story.title: A Bowl of Rice
story.kicker: A girl brings food to a tired man under a tree.
paragraphs: Buddhists tell this story. A thin, tired man sat under a tree. It was Siddhartha. For years he had eaten almost nothing. He was trying to find an answer.
A young woman named Sujata came down the path. She carried a bowl of rice cooked in milk. She saw the tired man. She gave him the bowl with both hands.
Siddhartha ate the rice. He felt strong again. The story says he thought, "Being so hungry did not help me. I need a better way."
He thanked Sujata. Then he walked to a big fig tree. He sat down under it. He decided to sit and think until he understood.
story.think: Why do you think the bowl of rice mattered so much?

lessons.title: Trying Very Hard
lessons.mainIdea: Buddhists tell that Siddhartha tried being very hungry, and it did not help.
reading: After he left the palace, Siddhartha looked for answers. Buddhists tell that he tried to be very hard on himself. He ate only a few grains a day.
He grew very thin and weak. He could hardly think. The story says he learned that hurting his body did not bring an answer.

words.d: not strong

look.title: Too Tired to Think
look.text: Look at a student who skipped breakfast. It is hard to listen. The words on the board look blurry. Her tummy growls.
look.prompt: Why is it hard to learn when you are very hungry?

check.why: Buddhists tell that he tried being very hungry and hard on himself.
The story says it made him weak and did not bring an answer.
Weak means not strong.

lessons.title: Sujata's Gift
lessons.mainIdea: A girl named Sujata gave Siddhartha a bowl of rice.
reading: Buddhists tell that a young woman named Sujata brought him rice cooked in milk. She shared her food with a stranger.
Siddhartha ate it and felt strong. Buddhists remember Sujata's kindness. Her small gift helped him on his way.

words.d: something you give to help or please someone

look.title: A Kind Act
look.text: Look at Sujata walking down the path. She holds a warm bowl with both hands. She sees a tired man. She stops and holds out the bowl.
look.prompt: What small gift could you give to help someone?

check.why: Buddhists tell that Sujata brought the bowl of rice.
The story says it was rice cooked in milk.
After eating, he felt strong enough to keep searching.

lessons.title: Not Too Much, Not Too Little
lessons.mainIdea: Buddhists call the path between too much and too little the middle way.
reading: In the palace, the prince had too much. In the forest, he had too little. Neither one helped him find his answer.
Buddhists say he found a middle way. It is not too much and not too little. The Buddha later taught this in his first talk.

words.d: the path between too much and too little

look.title: The Guitar String
look.text: Buddhists often tell this picture. A string that is too tight snaps. A string that is too loose makes no sound. A string that is just right makes music.
look.prompt: How is the string like the middle way?

choices: not too much, not too little
check.why: Buddhists describe the middle way as between too much and too little.

check.q: Where did the prince have too much?
check.why: In the palace he had riches and everything he wanted.

check.q: In the string picture, which string makes music?
check.why: The just-right string stands for the middle way.

lessons.title: The Middle Way Every Day
lessons.mainIdea: People can think about balance in everyday life.
reading: Buddhists use the middle way to think about many things. Eat enough, but not too much. Play hard, and rest too.
You can see balance in your day. Too much screen time feels bad. Too little sleep feels bad. Just enough helps.

words.d: just enough of each thing

look.title: A Balanced Plate
look.unit: parts of a plate out of 4 (about)
look.prompt: Which food takes up the most room on the plate?

check.why: Balance means just enough of each, like the middle way.
Balance is just enough of each thing.
Buddhists say the Buddha taught the middle way in his first talk.

lessons.title: Sitting Under the Tree
lessons.mainIdea: Buddhists believe Siddhartha understood under the tree and became the Buddha.
reading: Siddhartha sat under a big fig tree. He sat very still and thought for a long time. Buddhists tell that it was a full-moon night.
Buddhists believe that, by morning, he understood why people suffer and how it can end. From then on he was called the Buddha. Buddha means "the awakened one."

words.d: a title meaning "the awakened one"
woken up; Buddhists use it to mean seeing clearly

look.title: Waking Up
look.text: Think about waking up in the morning. Your eyes open. The room gets clear. Buddhists use "awake" as a picture word. They mean the Buddha's mind saw clearly.
look.prompt: Why might Buddhists use the word awake for this?

check.why: Buddha is a title meaning "the awakened one."
Buddhists tell that he sat under a fig tree, later called the Bodhi tree.

choices: he went back to the palace
he understood and became the Buddha
check.why: Buddhists believe he awakened under the tree.

lessons.title: The Bodhi Tree Today
lessons.mainIdea: A tree grown from a cutting of the old tree still grows in Bodh Gaya.
reading: The place is called Bodh Gaya, in India. The tree is called the Bodhi tree. Bodhi means awakening.
Buddhists say the tree there today grew from a cutting of the old one. Visitors come from all over the world. They bow and leave flowers to show respect.

words.d: the tree where Buddhists believe the Buddha awakened

look.title: A Visit to Bodh Gaya
look.text: Look at a big tree with heart-shaped leaves. Bright flags hang nearby. People sit quietly in its shade. Some bring flowers and set them down gently.
look.prompt: Why do you think people bring flowers to this tree?

check.why: The Bodhi tree grows at Bodh Gaya in India.
Bodhi means awakening.
Buddhists show respect with bows and flowers.

review.why: Buddhists tell that Sujata gave him a bowl of rice.

review.q: What did being very hungry teach him?
review.why: The story says hurting his body did not bring an answer.

choices: not too much, not too little
review.why: Buddhists call the path between too much and too little the middle way.

review.q: Where do Buddhists believe he awakened?
review.why: Buddhists believe he awakened under the Bodhi tree at Bodh Gaya.

review.q: Which string makes music in the story picture?
review.why: The just-right string is a picture of the middle way.
